title: Nahum 1:9–15
context: The prophet asks what they plot against the LORD, and answers that the LORD will make a full end; affliction will not rise up a second time. Those who plot are pictured as thorns and as dry stubble, consumed utterly; one has gone out who devises evil against the LORD and counsels wickedness. The LORD then says that though they are in full strength and many, they will be cut down and pass away; though he has afflicted his people, he will afflict them no more, and will break the yoke and burst the bonds. A command follows concerning the oppressor: no more descendants will bear the name, engraved and molten images will be cut off from the house of the gods, and a grave is made, for he is vile. The chapter closes with good news on the mountains for Judah: feasts may be kept and vows performed, for the wicked one will no more pass through and is utterly cut off. Isaiah 52:7 also speaks of the feet of one who brings good news; see that passage. The two are not merged. Versification: English 1:15 is Hebrew 2:1, and English 2:1–13 is Hebrew 2:2–14; this page keeps the WEB numbers.

verses.text: What do you plot against the LORD? He will make a full end. Affliction won’t rise up the second time.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prophet asks, “What do you plot against the LORD?” The answer is that the LORD will make a full end, and “Affliction won’t rise up the second time.” Many readers hear the “you” as Nineveh, and the affliction as what Judah will not have to bear again; the verse itself asks about plotting and promises a full end.

Arminian readers hear a real question to plotters, a warning that schemes against the LORD will not stand, and a word of relief that the affliction will not be allowed to rise twice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the plotting, the full end, and the word that affliction will not rise a second time as the LORD’s own appointed close to the trouble.

Shared ground: a full end is coming, and affliction will not rise up a second time. The plot against the LORD will not last.

verses.text: For entangled like thorns, and drunken as with their drink, they are consumed utterly like dry stubble.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For entangled like thorns, and drunken as with their drink, they are consumed utterly like dry stubble.” The plotters are compared to tangled thorns and to people drunken with their drink, and they are consumed like dry stubble. The images are of something ready to burn, and they are told in those comparisons, without a longer scene.

Arminian readers hear a people caught in their own tangle and their own drink, a consumption that answers the plot of the verse before, a warning still spoken in figures they can understand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the thorns, the drunkenness, and the utter consumption like dry stubble as the LORD’s appointed end for those who plot against him.

Shared ground: they are consumed utterly like dry stubble. The comparisons are the verse’s own, and they are enough.

verses.text: One has gone out of you who devises evil against the LORD, who counsels wickedness.
verses.arminianNotes:
“One has gone out of you who devises evil against the LORD, who counsels wickedness.” Someone has gone out from the city who devises evil against the LORD and counsels wickedness. Many readers take this as a leader from Nineveh; the verse does not name him. The charge is the devising and the counsel, aimed against the LORD.

Arminian readers hear a real counselor of wickedness, a person who has gone out from the people with a plot, and a word that still treats that counsel as guilt before the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the one who has gone out, the evildoing devised against the LORD, and the counsel of wickedness as the LORD’s own charge against that figure and the city he comes from.

Shared ground: one has gone out who devises evil against the LORD. The name is not given in the verse.

verses.text: The LORD says: “Though they are in full strength and likewise many, even so they will be cut down and pass away. Though I have afflicted you, I will afflict you no more.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Though they are in full strength and likewise many, even so they will be cut down and pass away. Though I have afflicted you, I will afflict you no more.” The LORD himself speaks. “They” are many and strong, yet they will be cut down; “you” have been afflicted, and that affliction will end. Many readers hear “they” as the oppressor and “you” as Judah; the verse itself shifts the pronouns and does not label each addressee.

Arminian readers hear a word of comfort spoken into real affliction, a promise that the many and the strong will pass away, and that the LORD will not go on afflicting his people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the LORD’s saying, the cutting down of the many and strong, and the end of affliction for “you” as his own sure word.

Shared ground: the strong will pass away, and the affliction of “you” will not continue. The LORD is the speaker of both lines.

verses.text: Now I will break his yoke from off you, and will burst your bonds apart.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now I will break his yoke from off you, and will burst your bonds apart.” The yoke and the bonds come off. “His” yoke is heard as the oppressor’s; “you” and “your bonds” continue the comfort of the verse before. The speech that began with “The LORD says” runs on through this promise.

Arminian readers hear a real breaking of a real yoke, a freeing of people who have been bound, and a “now” that treats the relief as the LORD’s timely act on their behalf.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the breaking of the yoke and the bursting of the bonds as the LORD’s own act, the other side of the cutting down already spoken.

Shared ground: the yoke is broken and the bonds are burst. The “you” of the promise is the people he will no longer afflict.

verses.text: The LORD has commanded concerning you: “No more descendants will bear your name. Out of the house of your gods, I will cut off the engraved image and the molten image. I will make your grave, for you are vile.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD has commanded concerning this “you”: “No more descendants will bear your name. Out of the house of your gods, I will cut off the engraved image and the molten image. I will make your grave, for you are vile.” The address turns. No more descendants will bear the name; images are cut off from the house of the gods; a grave is made, because this “you” is vile. Many readers hear the oppressor or the city here, not the Judah of the yoke; the verse is a command of ending, not of relief.

Arminian readers hear a final sentence on a named line and a house of gods, a grave prepared because of vileness, a word the oppressor can still recognize as the LORD’s command.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the command, the end of the name, the cutting off of the images, and the grave as the LORD’s own appointed end for that “you.”

Shared ground: the name, the images, and the future are cut off. The two “you” addresses of verses 12–14 sit side by side and are not forced into one label.

verses.text: Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you. He is utterly cut off.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you.” The good news is for Judah: feasts may be kept, vows performed, because the wicked one will no more pass through, and is utterly cut off. Isaiah 52:7 also speaks of the feet of one who brings good news; see that passage. The two are not merged.

Arminian readers hear a genuine gospel for Judah, peace published on the mountains, and a cut-off of the wicked one that makes room for worship to resume in safety.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the announcement on the mountains, the call to keep feasts and vows, and the utter cutting off of the wicked one as the LORD’s own good news for Judah.

Shared ground: good news and peace are published, and the wicked one will no more pass through Judah. Isaiah 52:7 stands beside the verse by reference.
